title: Multi-agent Collaboration with State Management
claim: A mediating layer between concurrent agents and shared state detects and resolves conflicts at write time, instead of deferring to merging.
layout: Top-to-bottom hub layout, manager bookends, numbered mediator stages, legend and workspace at bottom
description: A dense system diagram with a Manager Agent robot at the top left. It sends blue "Task Delegation" arrows to a central box of Parallel Engineer Agents. These are cartoon cat, dog and bunny coders, each with "Implement Task" and "Read / Write via STORM" boxes. A second Manager robot at top right receives "Results" and lists review, integrate and commit. Below the engineers, blue solid Read/Write Request arrows go down and green dashed Response arrows come back up. They connect to a green-bordered STORM Manager panel split into four numbered stages: Versioning, Validation with three checks (reservation, version, snapshot), On Success (green) and On Failure (red). At the bottom, a Shared Workspace strip shows a file tree and versioned Python files (utils.py v12, core.py v8, models.py v6). A legend sits at the bottom right. The eye goes first to the colorful mascots, then down to the STORM panel.
caption: System architecture. The manager analyzes the repository, delegates tasks to parallel engineers, and commits their work. All engineers share one workspace; the STORM manager mediates file operations to detect and resolve conflicts.
abstract: Recent advances in multi-agent systems have shown great potential for solving complex tasks. However, when multiple agents edit a shared codebase concurrently, their changes can silently conflict and inconsistent views lead to integration failures. Existing multi-agent systems address this through workspace isolation (e.g., one git worktree per agent), but this defers conflict resolution to a post-hoc merge step where recovery is expensive. In this paper, we propose STORM, i.e., STate-ORiented Management for multi-agent collaboration. Specifically, STORM manages agent states by mediating their interactions with the shared workspace, ensuring that each agent operates on a consistent view of the codebase and that conflicting edits are detected and resolved at write time. We evaluate STORM on Commit0 and PaperBench across multiple LLMs. STORM outperforms the git-worktree-based multi-agent baseline by +18.7 on Commit0-Lite and +1.4 on PaperBench, while achieving comparable or better cost efficiency. Combined with single-agent runs, STORM reaches highest scores of 87.6 and 78.2 on the two benchmarks respectively, suggesting that explicit state management is a more effective foundation for multi-agent collaboration than workspace isolation. STORM can also be plugged into any multi-agent system seamlessly.
